beats.lead: A 2,000-year-old seed grew into a living tree.
beats.text: In 2005, scientists germinated a date palm seed recovered decades earlier from the ruins of Masada, Israel, one of the oldest seeds ever known to sprout.
beats.note: The seed had been sitting in storage since the original excavation in the 1960s.

beats.name: Dr Sarah Sallon and Dr Elaine Solowey
beats.role: planted the ancient seed and coaxed it into germinating, then watched it grow into a healthy young date palm they named Methuselah.

beats.context: roughly the age of the seed that grew into Methuselah, and roughly how long it had been since a tree from this ancient line last bore fruit.

beats.text: Methuselah turned out to be male, so it could produce pollen but never fruit on its own. Researchers later germinated more ancient seeds from other sites, and some grew into female trees.
beats.note: Growing a 2,000-year-old seed at all was the hard part. Getting an actual harvest still took another cross of trees.

beats.text: One of those female trees, named Hannah, was hand-pollinated using Methuselah's pollen. By the early 2020s the cross had produced real dates grown from an ancient Judean seed line, something nobody had eaten in two thousand years.

beats.line: A seed sat still for 2,000 years, then someone finally planted it.
